**Document:** Efficacy and safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.
**Section:** Introduction

Neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by the progressive loss of neuronal structure and function and, due to the limited regenerative capacity of nervous tissue, constitute conditions with highly complex management . Although they encompass a broad spectrum, these disorders share certain elements, among which the death or inactivity of motor and/or sensory neurons and alterations in cerebral energy metabolism that contribute to neurotransmitter imbalance deserve particular emphasis . Among them, Parkinson’s disease (PD) is one of the most prevalent worldwide, affecting approximately 13.43 per 100,000 individuals (when age-standardized), thus representing the second most common neurodegenerative disease with advancing age . PD is a neurological condition caused by the progressive degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons, located predominantly in the pars compacta of the substantia nigra in the midbrain . This neurotransmitter modulates motor activity within the basal ganglia; therefore, its depletion in the striatum—the basis of PD pathophysiology—leads to dysregulation of this circuit, resulting in excessive inhibition of the thalamus and, consequently, of the motor cortex, giving rise to the cardinal symptoms of the disease, namely: bradykinesia, resting tremor, rigidity, and postural instability . Moreover, in addition to these typical motor alterations, the disease also manifests through non-motor symptoms such as hyposmia, sleep disturbances, constipation, depression, cognitive decline, among others, which often precede motor signs . In recent decades, the “gold-standard” treatment recommended for the disease has been the daily administration of levodopa (L-dopa), a dopamine precursor capable of crossing the blood–brain barrier and being converted within the central nervous system (CNS) into this neurotransmitter, thereby alleviating motor symptoms in these patients . Nevertheless, chronic L-dopa use is associated with motor fluctuations and the emergence of dyskinesias, involuntary movements that may become disabling . This limitation, together with the fact that there is currently no therapy that modifies the course of the disease, constitutes the main drivers of the search for new therapeutic approaches for PD . In this context, recent studies involving glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), originally used for the treatment of diabetes mellitus (DM), suggest a promising potential of these drugs in PD management . This hypothesis is supported, in part, by the fact that glucose is the primary energy source for nervous tissue and that alterations in its metabolism may already be present in the early stages of the disease . Such metabolic impairment has been related to mechanisms including insulin resistance, oxidative stress, and blood–brain barrier dysfunction, which hinder insulin signaling and promote mitochondrial dysfunction, leading to reduced efficiency of energy metabolism and negatively impacting the viability of dopaminergic neurons . In addition, insulin resistance is also believed to favor α-synuclein aggregation, which participates in PD pathophysiology and is notably neurotoxic . Within this framework, medications in this drug class, such as lixisenatide, liraglutide, and exenatide, have recently emerged in the medical field as potentially disease-modifying agents . In this study, we compared the effects of 2 commonly used levodopa combinations, LCE and LB, on dopamine levels in patients with early-stage (Hoehn and Yahr stages 1 and 1.5) idiopathic Parkinson’s disease. No significant differences were observed in dopamine levels between the 2 treatment groups at any of the 3 time points: before drug administration, 90 minutes, and 180 minutes post-dose. Furthermore, within-group analyses revealed no significant increase in dopamine levels over time in either treatment group. These findings suggest that in clinical practice, the 2 levodopa formulations often used interchangeably exhibit comparable biochemical efficacy in early-stage unilateral Parkinson’s disease. Both combinations appeared to increase dopamine levels to a similar extent, with this increase remaining within a limited range and showing no significant difference in the short-term follow-up following single-dose administration during the early stages of the disease. Levodopa remains the most effective agent for the treatment of motor symptoms in Parkinson’s; however, its chronic use is associated with the development of motor complications. Growing evidence suggests that the short half-life of levodopa and the resulting pulsatile stimulation of striatal dopamine receptors contribute to diminished therapeutic efficacy, motor fluctuations, and dyskinesia. DDCI, such as carbidopa or benserazide, is co-administered with levodopa to reduce peripheral dopamine conversion, minimize nausea, and enhance central bioavailability. Adding a COMT inhibitor to the levodopa–DDCI combination can further prolong the peripheral half-life of levodopa and improve its central bioavailability. The addition of entacapone to levodopa therapy reduces motor complications by extending the half-life of the drug. For instance, a study conducted by Kuoppamäki et al demonstrated that the LCE combination provided a higher minimum plasma concentration and a greater area under the curve than LC alone. These pharmacokinetic advantages are believed to contribute to the delayed onset of motor complications. In a meta-analysis, treatment with LCE was shown to improve scores on the Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) Part II, UPDRS Part III, and Schwab and England Activities of Daily Living scale compared with LB therapy in patients with Parkinson’s disease. However, no significant differences were observed between the 2 treatments in terms of the UPDRS part I, UPDRS part IV, frequency of end-of-dose wearing-off, or quality of life scores measured by the PDQ-39 or PDQ-8. question: What is the role of levodopa in Parkinson's disease management?
answer:
### Main Topic: Levodopa in Parkinson's Disease Management

Levodopa plays a crucial role in the management of Parkinson's disease (PD) as the primary treatment for motor symptoms, particularly for bradykinesia, rigidity, and tremors. It is often used in combination with carbidopa to enhance its efficacy and reduce peripheral side effects.

#### Core Clinical Concepts:

• **Levodopa Mechanism of Action:** Levodopa is a precursor to dopamine, which is converted into dopamine in the brain by the enzyme dopa decarboxylase. This increase in dopamine levels helps to alleviate the dopaminergic deficiency characteristic of PD. The combination of levodopa and carbidopa inhibits peripheral dopa decarboxylase, thereby reducing the conversion of levodopa to dopamine outside the brain and increasing the amount of levodopa that crosses the blood-brain barrier.

• **Clinical Presentation and Semiology:** The primary motor symptoms of PD include tremors, bradykinesia (slowness of movement), rigidity, and postural instability. Levodopa is particularly effective in improving bradykinesia and rigidity, but its efficacy for tremors is more variable. The "on-off" phenomenon, where patients experience fluctuations in motor symptoms, is a common issue with long-term levodopa use.

• **Diagnostic Criteria and Monitoring:** The diagnosis of PD is primarily clinical, based on the presence of characteristic motor symptoms and the absence of other causes. Monitoring of levodopa therapy includes regular assessments of motor function, as well as monitoring for potential side effects such as dyskinesias, hallucinations, and orthostatic hypotension.

• **Evidence-Based Management Principles:** Levodopa is typically initiated when motor symptoms become disabling, and its use is tailored to the individual patient's needs. The goal is to achieve optimal control of motor symptoms while minimizing side effects. Strategies for managing levodopa-related side effects include adjusting the dosage, using other dopaminergic medications, and employing behavioral interventions.

• **Pharmacological Classes and Clinical Trade-Offs:** Levodopa is a dopamine precursor, and its use is associated with several clinical trade-offs. While it is highly effective for motor symptoms, long-term use can lead to complications such as dyskinesias, hallucinations, and motor fluctuations. The decision to use levodopa should be made in consultation with a healthcare provider, taking into account the patient's individual needs and the potential risks and benefits of therapy.

question: How is epilepsy distinguished from a single provoked seizure?
answer:
### Main Topic: Distinction Between Epilepsy and Single Provoked Seizures

Epilepsy is defined as a chronic neurological condition characterized by an enduring predisposition to generate unprovoked seizures, whereas a single provoked seizure is an acute, symptomatic event triggered by a transient systemic or environmental insult. The clinical distinction relies on the assessment of seizure recurrence risk, which is significantly higher in epilepsy compared to the transient nature of a provoked event.

#### Core Clinical Concepts:

• **Defining Epilepsy (The ILAE Criteria):** According to the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE), a diagnosis of epilepsy is established if a patient meets any of the following: (1) at least two unprovoked (or reflex) seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart; (2) one unprovoked (or reflex) seizure and a probability of further seizures similar to the general recurrence risk (at least 60%) after two unprovoked seizures, occurring over the next 10 years; or (3) a diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome. This framework shifts the focus from a purely descriptive definition to one that incorporates the statistical likelihood of future events.

• **Pathophysiology of Provoked Seizures:** Provoked seizures, often termed acute symptomatic seizures, occur in the setting of a temporary brain insult. Common triggers include metabolic disturbances (e.g., severe hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, uremia), toxic exposures (e.g., drug withdrawal, stimulant overdose), or acute structural injuries (e.g., acute ischemic stroke, traumatic brain injury, or intracranial hemorrhage). The mechanism involves a transient lowering of the seizure threshold due to acute neurochemical or ionic imbalances, which typically resolves once the underlying systemic or environmental factor is corrected.

• **The Role of Epileptogenesis:** Epilepsy involves a permanent alteration in neuronal network excitability, often resulting from prior brain injury, genetic predisposition, or developmental malformations. This process, known as epileptogenesis, involves structural changes such as axonal sprouting, synaptic reorganization, and glial activation that create a chronic state of hyperexcitability. In contrast, a provoked seizure does not necessarily imply that the brain has undergone these permanent network changes, meaning the patient may not require long-term antiseizure medication (ASM) once the acute trigger is removed.

• **Diagnostic Evaluation and Risk Stratification:** Distinguishing between the two requires a comprehensive diagnostic workup, including neuroimaging (MRI to identify structural lesions like mesial temporal sclerosis or cortical dysplasia) and electroencephalography (EEG). An EEG showing interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) significantly increases the risk of recurrence, supporting an epilepsy diagnosis even after a single unprovoked seizure. Conversely, if the EEG is normal and the seizure was clearly linked to a transient trigger (e.g., alcohol withdrawal), the event is classified as a provoked seizure, and the patient is generally not considered to have epilepsy.

• **Management Principles and Clinical Trade-offs:** The management of a provoked seizure focuses exclusively on treating the underlying cause (e.g., correcting electrolyte levels or managing withdrawal), and ASMs are typically not indicated for long-term use. In contrast, the management of epilepsy involves a risk-benefit analysis regarding the initiation of chronic ASM therapy. Clinicians must weigh the risk of recurrent seizures—which carry risks of injury, status epilepticus, and psychosocial impact—against the potential side effects, drug-drug interactions, and teratogenicity associated with long-term pharmacological intervention.

### Main Topic: Distinction Between Epilepsy and Single Provoked Seizures

Epilepsy is a chronic neurological condition defined by an enduring predisposition to generate unprovoked seizures [S3, S9]. In contrast, a single provoked seizure—often referred to as an acute symptomatic seizure—is a transient event triggered by a specific, acute systemic or neurological insult [S1, S4]. The primary clinical distinction lies in the risk of recurrence: epilepsy is diagnosed when there is a high probability of future seizures, whereas a provoked seizure is typically considered a one-time event that resolves once the underlying trigger is addressed [S1, S4, S9].

#### Supporting Clinical Evidence:

*   **Diagnostic Criteria for Epilepsy:** According to the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE), a diagnosis of epilepsy is established if a patient meets any of the following: (1) at least two unprovoked (or reflex) seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart; (2) one unprovoked seizure with a high probability of recurrence (at least 60% over the next 10 years, comparable to the risk after two unprovoked seizures); or (3) a diagnosis of a specific epilepsy syndrome [S3, S8, S9].
*   **Defining Provoked (Acute Symptomatic) Seizures:** Provoked seizures occur in close temporal proximity to an acute brain insult, such as stroke, traumatic brain injury, anoxic encephalopathy, or metabolic/toxic disturbances [S1, S4]. While the ILAE has historically used a 7-day window for structural insults (like stroke or trauma) and a 24-hour window for metabolic/toxic causes to categorize these as "acute symptomatic," these thresholds are considered somewhat arbitrary and are primarily intended for epidemiological standardization rather than individual clinical management [S1].
*   **Clinical Management and Recurrence Risk:** Unlike epilepsy, where antiseizure medication (ASM) is often indicated to prevent further events, ASMs are not routinely started after a single unprovoked seizure unless there is a high recurrence risk (e.g., structural brain lesion or confirmed epilepsy syndrome) [S6]. In cases of provoked seizures, the focus is on treating the underlying systemic or structural cause, as the risk of subsequent unprovoked seizures is generally lower than in patients with established epilepsy [S1, S4, S6].
*   **Diagnostic Workup:** Because the distinction between these categories is critical for long-term prognosis, clinical guidelines (such as NICE NG217, 2022) recommend an urgent specialist assessment for any suspected first seizure [S6]. This includes a detailed eyewitness history, a 12-lead ECG to rule out cardiac syncope, and neuroimaging (preferably MRI) to identify structural causes, as these findings significantly influence the classification of the event and the necessity for long-term treatment [S3, S6].

**Document:** Post-stroke seizures: classification, risk prediction, and management.
**Section:** The 7-day rule: origin and intended purpose

The distinction between a seizure provoked by an acute brain injury and the onset of epilepsy predates the 7-day rule by several decades. Before the 1980s, operational windows ranged from 24 h to several weeks, depending on the cohort and research question. Jennett’s studies of non-missile head injury, published in 1969 and 1973, introduced the first explicit 1-week definition of an early seizure (4, 5). The Rochester Epidemiology Project reports of 1993 and 1995 applied the same interval within a provoked-versus-unprovoked framework encompassing stroke, traumatic brain injury, and central nervous system infection (6, 7). Two later Rochester analyses, published in 1998 and 2009, provided the principal empirical basis for the distinction: among 10-year survivors of a first acute symptomatic seizure, the cumulative risk of a subsequent unprovoked seizure was substantially lower than after a first unprovoked seizure and varied markedly according to status epilepticus and aetiology (8, 9). Other cohorts of the same period used different definitions. The Oxfordshire Community Stroke Project (1997) and the Bladin multicentre study (2000) applied a 2-week window (10, 11), whereas the Rochester cerebral infarction study of So and colleagues (1996) retained 1 week (12). This inconsistency impeded comparisons across cohorts and prompted the ILAE Task Force, in 2010, to recommend 7 days for stroke, traumatic brain injury, and anoxic encephalopathy, and 24 h for metabolic and toxic causes (2). Table 1 lists the pre-2010 definitions in chronological order, together with the two sources cited by the Task Force for cerebrovascular disease. Three aspects of the 2010 document warrant emphasis. First, its stated purpose was epidemiological. The Task Force wrote that the definition “was created for use in epidemiologic studies” and that acute symptomatic seizures should be “separately categorized for epidemiologic purposes” (2). The objective was to standardise cohorts, not to determine whether an individual patient should be discharged on antiseizure medication. Second, the Task Force did not claim biological precision. It stated that “the criteria for acute symptomatic seizures are somewhat arbitrary” and described the document as “a first attempt to codify the levels of risk associated with a broad spectrum of insults” (2). Describing the 7-day threshold as arbitrary therefore reiterates a limitation acknowledged by its authors. Third, the Task Force explicitly anticipated further refinement: “further definition of timing of seizures in relation to the acute event is necessary, and further refinement may be possible after taking into account clinical factors associated with neurologic insults (i.e., severity of trauma for head injury; area of the lesion for cerebrovascular disease)” (2). Lesion-based refinement in stroke was therefore part of the original research agenda. The empirical support for the exact interval is more limited than its widespread adoption might imply. For cerebrovascular disease, the 2010 Task Force cited Jennett and colleagues’ 1973 head-injury data (5) and the 2004 narrative review by Camilo and Goldstein (13); neither source compared the 7-day threshold with alternative intervals in stroke. Subsequent cohort studies have generally adopted the threshold by reference, and, to our knowledge, no study has systematically validated

neurologic insults (i.e., severity of trauma for head injury; area of the lesion for cerebrovascular disease)” (2). Lesion-based refinement in stroke was therefore part of the original research agenda. The empirical support for the exact interval is more limited than its widespread adoption might imply. For cerebrovascular disease, the 2010 Task Force cited Jennett and colleagues’ 1973 head-injury data (5) and the 2004 narrative review by Camilo and Goldstein (13); neither source compared the 7-day threshold with alternative intervals in stroke. Subsequent cohort studies have generally adopted the threshold by reference, and, to our knowledge, no study has systematically validated it against competing definitions. The few direct comparisons have produced conflicting proposals: 14 days, on the basis of incidence density in a 2018 meta-analysis (14), and 3 days, on the basis of progression risk in a 2021 cohort study (15). Fifteen years after the Task Force document, the evidence has not materially resolved this question. The ILAE has assigned revision of the acute symptomatic seizure definition to a dedicated working group, separate from the 2025 update of seizure classification (16). A related argument was advanced in 2026 for acute status epilepticus, in which structurally and systemically provoked cases are grouped by temporal proximity despite differing mechanisms and outcomes (17).

### [Layer 3 > Epilepsy > Introduction > Stem cell-based therapeutics in epilepsy: current advances and future prospects.]
**Document:** Stem cell-based therapeutics in epilepsy: current advances and future prospects.
**Section:** Introduction

Epilepsy is a common neurological disorder with a global prevalence of approximately 600 per 100 000, affecting more than 50 million individuals worldwide.1,2 Seizures occur from abnormal synchronous neuronal firing involving focal or diffuse cortical networks, triggered by structural, infectious, or metabolic perturbations. Epilepsy manifests as a complex disorder with environmental effects acting on inherited susceptibility, mediated by common variation in particular genes, rather than a single mutation or cause.1 Diverse causes of epilepsy result in a bimodal distribution, with genetic causes in childhood and accumulated injury to the brain (eg, trauma, tumors) in the elderly.2 As epilepsy displays a wide range of possible pathophysiological features, from well-recognized convulsions to psychological symptoms, a detailed history serves as the cornerstone of the diagnosis.1 Additional tests such as electroencephalogram (EEG) and neuroimaging, preferably magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), help identify the structural and functional causes, facilitating diagnosis and classification of epilepsy.3,4 The International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) defines epilepsy by any of the following conditions: (1) At least two unprovoked seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart; (2) one unprovoked seizure and a probability of further seizures at least 60% (ie, comparable to recurrent risk after two unprovoked seizures) over the next 10 years; (3) diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome.5 Epilepsy is classified into four main classes: Focal, Generalized, Combined, and Unknown.6 Patients with generalized epilepsy exhibit generalized spike-wave activity on EEG, whereas focal epilepsy shows epileptiform activity that is confined to a single hemisphere. The combined epilepsy, such as Dravet syndrome and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, is defined by both generalized spike-wave and focal epileptiform discharges during seizure. Lastly, the unknown group refers to cases where epilepsy is confirmed but the type cannot be determined due to insufficient information, such as an unavailable or uninformative EEG. Noteworthy, epilepsy may involve multiple seizure types in the same patient. Progress in genomic technology is exposing the complex genetic architecture of the common types of epilepsy, facilitating more precise classification and treatment design.1,7 Epilepsy greatly reduces quality of life and poses a risk of a sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP).7 Current antiseizure medications (ASMs) depend on inhibition of sodium channel or calcium channel, enhancement of gamma-aminobutyric acid-related (GABAergic) inhibition, and glutamate-mediated excitation blockage.7 However, ASMs are effective in 60%-70% of individuals and only suppress seizures but not the underlying epileptogenesis, resulting in an unchanged long-term prognosis.7 Apart from frequent adverse effects that limit tolerance, and thus, the efficacy of ASMs, approximately 30% of epileptic patients are resistant to treatment despite accurate diagnosis and carefully monitored drug levels.7 Epilepsy surgery appears as the most effective way to achieve long-term seizure remission, up to 30%-60%, for patients with focal epilepsy refractory to medications.1 Nonetheless, epilepsy surgery remains significantly underutilized due to the requirement for extensive evaluations and specialized expertise.8 Consequently, many novel treatments have emerged in the past decades, aiming to suppress underlying epileptogenesis and restore damaged neural circuits.

### [Layer 3 > Epilepsy > INTRODUCTION > Seizure relapse in new onset epilepsy: It is not always drug resistance.]
**Document:** Seizure relapse in new onset epilepsy: It is not always drug resistance.
**Section:** INTRODUCTION

Epileptic seizures occur in approximately 8%–10% of the population. 1 Most studies reported 40%–50% relapses at 2 years, 2 , 3 , 4 although lower numbers (27%) have been also found in older studies. 5 Whereas some research has investigated specific causes of relapse, such as poor adherence, 6 a comprehensive understanding of the distribution of different causes of relapse in the first years after the onset of epilepsy remains limited. First‐time seizures can be divided into four main categories: symptoms of new onset epilepsy (NOE), unprovoked epileptic seizures in patients not fulfilling the criteria for epilepsy diagnosis, acute symptomatic seizures (ASyS; formerly also called “provoked seizures”), and manifestations of nonepileptic events (such as syncope or functional/dissociative seizures). It is known that the recurrence rate depends critically on correct diagnosis and appropriate treatment. However, there are few studies on the precise causes of recurrence after the first seizure. In patients with NOE, a seizure recurrence may be due to ineffective treatment, but also to poor adherence to therapy, inadequate treatment, low drug levels, ASyS, or nonepileptic events. Furthermore, not all recurrences in a single patient have the same cause. Investigating relapses is important, because they carry a similar risk of morbidity and mortality as the first attack and can be mistaken for ineffective treatment. In this study, based on our registry of consecutive patients with NOE diagnosis in the Canton of Geneva, we investigated the causes of each relapse, their changes over time, and the emergence of drug resistance to one or two medications within the first 5 years after epilepsy diagnosis. All patients underwent comprehensive examinations from the time they were enrolled in our registry, thus providing a unique opportunity to explore the true prevalence of drug resistance.

### [Layer 2 > Epilepsy > NICE NG217 > NICE NG217: Epilepsies in Children, Young People and Adults - First Seizure and Diagnosis]
**Document:** NICE NG217: Epilepsies in Children, Young People and Adults - First Seizure and Diagnosis
**Section:** First Seizure and Diagnosis

NICE guideline NG217 recommends that anyone presenting with a suspected first unprovoked seizure be referred urgently to a specialist with expertise in epilepsy, seen within 2 weeks. Diagnostic workup should include a detailed eyewitness history, 12-lead ECG to rule out cardiac syncope, and brain MRI using an epilepsy protocol. EEG is indicated to support classification, but a normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy. Antiseizure medication should not routinely be started after a single unprovoked seizure unless the person has an unequivocal epileptic syndrome, a structural brain lesion, or high recurrence risk (>60%).

### [Layer 3 > Epilepsy > Introduction > Genetic Diagnosis in Epilepsy: Implications for Clinical Management.]
**Document:** Genetic Diagnosis in Epilepsy: Implications for Clinical Management.
**Section:** Introduction

Epilepsy is a common neurological condition affecting 1–3% of the population worldwide and is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality . Epilepsy is most broadly defined as a predisposition to spontaneous seizures. It is clinically defined as two or more unprovoked seizures > 24 h apart, one unprovoked seizure with additional clinical factors conferring risk of developing additional seizures, or a diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome . In actuality, epilepsy is multiple disorders with a shared predominant symptom, so it is better described as “the epilepsies” . There are numerous causes of epilepsy including structural, infectious, metabolic, and traumatic, but it is now believed that the majority of unexplained epilepsy has a genetic contribution . Over the past 25 years, the importance of genetic testing in those with unexplained epilepsy has been increasingly recognized to impact clinical management and is now recommended to be part of routine clinical care.

The formal definition of epilepsy has been refined several times since 1981 . Specifically, ILAE and the International Bureau for Epilepsy (IBE) defined epilepsy in 2005, as “a disorder of the brain characterized by an enduring predisposition to generate epileptic seizures and by the neurobiologic, cognitive, psychological, and social consequences of this condition” . We attributed a diagnosis of “epilepsy” to a study population if the diagnosis was assigned based on any version of the ILAE definition, on a definition reported in a previous research article or on expert opinion. Accordingly, the term “people with epilepsy (PWE)” refers to individuals whose clinical manifestations met one of the diagnostic criteria for epilepsy described above.

### Main Topic: Distinguishing Epilepsy from a Single Provoked Seizure

A single provoked seizure is typically distinguished from epilepsy by the presence of a clear precipitating cause, such as a head injury, infection, or medication side effect, which resolves once the underlying cause is addressed. In contrast, epilepsy is characterized by recurrent, unprovoked seizures that are often unpredictable and may be associated with underlying neurological abnormalities.

#### Core Clinical Concepts:

• **Epilepsy Diagnosis:** The diagnosis of epilepsy is based on the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) criteria, which require the occurrence of at least two unprovoked seizures that are not part of a single acute symptomatic seizure episode. The ILAE also emphasizes the importance of identifying underlying causes of seizures, such as structural brain abnormalities, genetic predispositions, or metabolic disorders.

• **Provoked vs. Unprovoked Seizures:** Provoked seizures are those that occur in response to a specific precipitating cause, such as a head injury, infection, or medication side effect. Unprovoked seizures, on the other hand, occur without an identifiable cause and are often associated with underlying neurological abnormalities. The distinction between provoked and unprovoked seizures is critical in determining the underlying cause of seizures and guiding treatment decisions.

• **Clinical Presentation:** The clinical presentation of a single provoked seizure typically involves a clear precipitating cause, such as a head injury or infection, followed by a seizure that is often stereotypical and may be associated with a postictal phase. In contrast, epilepsy is often characterized by recurrent seizures that may be unpredictable and may be associated with underlying neurological abnormalities, such as structural brain lesions or genetic predispositions.

• **Diagnostic Criteria:** The diagnosis of epilepsy requires a comprehensive evaluation, including a detailed medical history, physical examination, and diagnostic tests, such as electroencephalography (EEG), imaging studies (e.g., MRI, CT), and laboratory tests (e.g., blood chemistry, genetic testing). The ILAE criteria emphasize the importance of identifying underlying causes of seizures and guiding treatment decisions based on the underlying pathophysiology.

• **Management Principles:** The management of a single provoked seizure typically involves addressing the underlying precipitating cause, such as discontinuing offending medications or treating underlying infections. In contrast, the management of epilepsy often involves long-term antiepileptic medication (AED) therapy, lifestyle modifications, and in some cases, surgical interventions or other adjunctive therapies.

• **Clinical Trade-Offs:** The distinction between epilepsy and a single provoked seizure has significant clinical implications, including the need for long-term AED therapy, lifestyle modifications, and in some cases, surgical interventions. question: What information does electroencephalography contribute to epilepsy evaluation?
answer:
### Main Topic: The Role of Electroencephalography (EEG) in Epilepsy Evaluation

Electroencephalography (EEG) serves as the gold-standard diagnostic tool for epilepsy by providing objective evidence of cortical hyperexcitability, allowing clinicians to classify seizure types, identify epilepsy syndromes, and localize the epileptogenic zone. It functions as a functional neuroimaging modality that captures the temporal dynamics of neuronal synchronization, which is essential for distinguishing epileptic seizures from non-epileptic paroxysmal events.

#### Core Clinical Concepts:

• **Detection of Interictal Epileptiform Discharges (IEDs):** The primary utility of routine EEG lies in the identification of IEDs, such as spikes, sharp waves, or spike-and-wave complexes, which represent localized or generalized hypersynchronous neuronal activity. While the presence of IEDs significantly increases the probability of an epilepsy diagnosis, their absence does not exclude it, as the sensitivity of a single routine EEG is relatively low (approximately 30-50%). Repeated studies, sleep-deprived EEGs, or prolonged ambulatory monitoring are often employed to increase the yield of capturing these transient markers.

• **Classification of Seizure Types and Epilepsy Syndromes:** EEG patterns are pathognomonic for specific epilepsy syndromes, which is critical for guiding pharmacological management. For instance, the presence of 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave discharges is highly characteristic of Childhood Absence Epilepsy, while generalized polyspike-and-wave activity may suggest Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy. By identifying the electrographic signature, clinicians can avoid prescribing anti-seizure medications (ASMs) that might exacerbate specific syndromes, such as avoiding sodium channel blockers in certain generalized genetic epilepsies.

• **Localization of the Epileptogenic Zone:** In patients being evaluated for epilepsy surgery, EEG is indispensable for mapping the cortical region responsible for seizure onset. Video-EEG monitoring (VEM) allows for the correlation of clinical semiology with electrographic changes, helping to determine if the seizures are focal or generalized. High-density EEG or intracranial EEG (iEEG) using subdural grids or stereotactic depth electrodes (SEEG) can further refine the localization of the seizure focus, providing the spatial resolution necessary to plan resective or ablative surgical interventions.

• **Differential Diagnosis of Paroxysmal Events:** EEG is the definitive tool for distinguishing epileptic seizures from non-epileptic paroxysmal events, such as psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES), syncope, or parasomnias. During a PNES event, the EEG typically remains normal or shows only movement-related artifacts, whereas an epileptic seizure is almost invariably accompanied by a clear, evolving electrographic change (rhythmic discharge, attenuation, or post-ictal slowing). This distinction is vital to prevent the inappropriate and potentially harmful long-term use of ASMs in patients with non-epileptic conditions.

• **Assessment of Post-Ictal and Background Activity:** Beyond identifying spikes, the analysis of background rhythm and post-ictal changes provides insight into overall cortical health. Focal slowing (delta or theta activity) in the interictal period often points to structural abnormalities or underlying cortical dysfunction in the region of the seizure focus. Furthermore, the observation of post-ictal suppression or focal slowing immediately following a clinical event provides strong evidence for the focal nature of the seizure, aiding in the lateralization and localization of the underlying pathology.

• **Clinical Trade-offs and Limitations:** While EEG is powerful, it is limited by its spatial resolution, as it primarily records activity from the cortical surface and is less sensitive to deep-seated foci (e.g., mesial temporal or orbitofrontal). Furthermore, the "interictal" nature of most recordings means that the absence of findings is common. Clinicians must balance the cost and resource intensity of prolonged monitoring against the clinical necessity of confirming a diagnosis or localizing a focus, always interpreting EEG data within the context of the patient's clinical history, semiology, and neuroimaging findings.

question: What information does electroencephalography contribute to epilepsy evaluation?
answer:
### Main Topic: The Role of Electroencephalography (EEG) in Epilepsy Evaluation

Electroencephalography (EEG) is considered a gold-standard diagnostic tool for epilepsy, providing essential electrophysiological data to classify seizure types, identify epilepsy syndromes, and localize the epileptogenic zone for surgical planning [S3, S7, S9]. By capturing the temporal dynamics of neuronal synchronization, EEG allows clinicians to identify objective evidence of cortical hyperexcitability, which is vital for distinguishing epileptic seizures from non-epileptic paroxysmal events [S9].

#### Supporting Clinical Evidence:

*   **Diagnostic Classification and Syndrome Identification:** EEG is fundamental in differentiating between generalized and focal epilepsy syndromes [S5, S7]. It identifies characteristic patterns, such as generalized spike-and-wave discharges in genetic generalized epilepsy (GGE), and helps recognize complex electroclinical patterns like "generalized onset seizures with focal evolution" (GOFE), which can otherwise lead to the inappropriate use of narrow-spectrum medications [S5, S7].
*   **Presurgical Localization:** In drug-resistant epilepsy, EEG—often integrated with other modalities like MRI, PET, and magnetoencephalography (MEG)—is used to define the epileptogenic zone [S1, S2]. Advanced techniques, such as electromagnetic source imaging (EMSI), combine EEG and MEG data to improve the spatial accuracy of source localization, helping to guide invasive monitoring (e.g., stereo-EEG) and surgical resection [S1, S2].
*   **Monitoring and Management:** Video-EEG (VEEG) monitoring is particularly valuable for capturing subtle clinical manifestations that may be missed by patients, providing a more accurate assessment of seizure burden [S3, S5]. It is also used to monitor treatment response to immunotherapy in autoimmune-associated epilepsy and to evaluate the efficacy of antiseizure medications [S3, S5].
*   **Advanced Electrophysiological Insights:** Beyond standard clinical recordings, intracranial EEG (iEEG) allows for the study of high-frequency oscillations and ultrafast electrical events (up to 8 kHz) [S6]. These microscopic-level recordings provide deeper insights into the pathophysiology of epileptic disorders and the functional significance of specific brain oscillations, which may eventually refine surgical and therapeutic strategies [S6].

### [Layer 3 > Epilepsy > INTRODUCTION > Magnetoencephalographic source imaging improves localization of the epileptogenic zone in multimodal imaging evaluation.]
**Document:** Magnetoencephalographic source imaging improves localization of the epileptogenic zone in multimodal imaging evaluation.
**Section:** INTRODUCTION

Presurgical evaluation of drug‐resistant focal epilepsy requires the integration of clinical, electrophysiological, and imaging data to accurately define the epileptogenic zone, the cortical area whose resection is necessary to achieve seizure freedom. 1 , 2 High‐resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and interictal fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography (FDG‐PET) are used routinely to identify lesions or hypometabolic regions that can guide intracranial exploration and surgical planning. 2 , 3 Magnetoencephalographic source imaging (MSI), which applies source localization algorithms to magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings, has emerged as a valuable non‐invasive tool for localizing interictal epileptiform discharges with high spatiotemporal resolution. 4 , 5 , 6 MSI plays an increasingly strategic role in stereo–electroencephalography (SEEG) planning by refining implantation hypotheses 5 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 to influence candidate selection for SEEG. A focal, plausible MSI source may support the decision to proceed with invasive monitoring, whereas non‐localizing MSI findings might prompt alternative management. 9 Despite its growing clinical use, MSI is still often viewed as a second‐line investigation. Its precise added value compared to MRI and PET remains unclear, and it is not systematically integrated into presurgical workflows. Whether MSI provides truly complementary information or simply confirms findings from other modalities has not been rigorously assessed. 11 This study aims to determine the specific contribution of MSI by comparing its localizing value to that of MRI and PET in a cohort of patients who underwent SEEG. We evaluate whether MSI identifies regions overlapping with SEEG‐defined seizure‐onset zones (SOZs) and resected tissue, and whether it offers additive information. Notably, MRI and PET were analyzed using both standard visual inspection and advanced post‐processing: morphometric analysis programs (MAP) for MRI, 12 , 13 and statistical parametric mapping (SPM) for PET. 14 We hypothesize that MSI provides added value for localizing the SOZ and resected area, as it captures a specific electrophysiological signature of epilepsy complementary to structural MRI lesions or metabolic PET abnormalities. Standard protocol approvals, registrations, and patient consents. Ethics Committee agreement was obtained for the study (CCP Lyon Sud Est IV Research Ethics Committee, approval number: N2012‐A00516‐37, 05/24/2012) in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Patients were fully informed and signed a written consent form.

**Document:** Autoimmune-associated epilepsy: definitions and diagnosis - a narrative review.
**Section:** ADDITIONAL TESTS IN THE DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

In AAE patients, EEG remains a useful tool to evaluate encephalopathy, epileptiform discharges, and seizure activity. However, there are no EEG patterns specific enough to reliably identify AAE outside the context of autoimmune encephalitis. 33 The ‘extreme delta brush’ pattern, for example, is considered characteristic of anti-NMDAR encephalitis, but it is not typically observed in other antibody-associated epilepsies. On the other hand, VEEG monitoring is particularly informative. Subtle clinical manifestations may go unnoticed by patients, resulting in an underestimation of seizure frequency; VEEG provides a more accurate assessment of seizure burden, and it is also valuable for monitoring treatment response to immunotherapy and ASMs. 1 22 Brain MRI remains a cornerstone in the evaluation of epilepsy, supported by well-established guidelines by the ILAE. Repeat imaging using the harmonized neuroimaging of epilepsy structural sequences (HARNESS)-MRI protocol—which includes high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) T1-weighted, 3D fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), and two-dimensional (2D) coronal T2-weighted sequences—is recommended in cases in which previous MRI is unavailable or suboptimal. Importantly, neuroimaging findings should be interpreted in conjunction with electroclinical data, especially in the context of unexplained seizure worsening, rapid cognitive decline, or new-onset neuropsychiatric symptoms. 34 Positron emission tomography and computed tomography with 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG), which assesses regional cerebral glucose metabolism, can offer additional diagnostic information. This technique is widely used in the evaluation of brain tumors and inflammatory disorders. 35 In AAE, most available data focus on cases of autoimmune encephalitis or acute symptomatic seizures. For the early detection of inflammatory brain involvement, PET-CT has been proposed as a modality more sensitive than MRI. 35 36 Inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) may be elevated in infectious or systemic inflammatory states. While nonspecific, some diagnostic protocols 37 include these markers as part of the workup, particularly to screen for systemic autoimmune or inflammatory conditions. Several systemic autoantibodies have also been investigated in epilepsy. In a 2015 observational study 38 involving 319 patients without known autoimmune disease, the presence of antinuclear antibodies (ANA), anti-β2-glycoprotein 1, anticardiolipin IgG, antimicrosomal antibodies, and antithyroglobulin was evaluated. At least one autoantibody was detected in 23.5% of the participants, with the following prevalences: anticardiolipin (9.4%), antimicrosomal (7.5%), ANA (5.6%), anti-β2-glycoprotein (5.6%), and antithyroglobulin (3.25%). Regarding the role of anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies, a study 39 comparing the prevalence of antithyroid antibodies in 42 patients with adult-onset TLE, stratified by known and unknown etiology, found a higher frequency of anti-TPO positivity among patients with unknown etiology. Furthermore, late-onset TLE associated with antithyroid antibodies tended to occur in middle-aged women and was frequently accompanied by cognitive decline and other autoimmune disorders, including anti-GAD65 positivity. 39 However, anti-TPO antibodies are relatively common in the general population (particularly among women), and their presence may represent an epiphenomenon rather than a direct pathogenic mechanism. Thus, although these findings contribute to the ongoing debate regarding the controversial role of anti-TPO antibodies in steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis (SREAT), anti-TPO positivity alone should not be considered evidence of AAE. This electroclinical pattern has been described in patients with GGE. The cohort of patients with GOFE studied in our institution were all females; this is a meaningful finding. We have no explanation for this, however, including our cases, 60% are females, 28% males, and 12% unknown (see Table S2). More work is needed to determine why females may be more at risk of this pattern. ### [Layer 3 > Epilepsy > INTRODUCTION > Ultrafast oscillations in the human brain and their functional significance.]
**Document:** Ultrafast oscillations in the human brain and their functional significance.
**Section:** INTRODUCTION

Using direct electrical signal recordings from the human brain via intracranial electrodes, a wide range of frequencies spanning from ultraslow (<.5 Hz) to very fast oscillations (500–2000 Hz) have been repeatedly detected. 1 , 2 All these electrophysiological phenomena can be observed in both healthy and functionally impaired brain structures using standard clinical macroelectrodes (1–10 mm2) to record local field potentials that reflected the summated synaptic and action potential activity, commonly called intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG). 3 In parallel, some studies with clinical macroelectrodes suggest that the human brain can generate even higher frequencies (>2 kHz). 4 , 5 , 6 If this is true, then EEG microrecordings, which remove volume averaging, should be a more potent tool to probe for these ultrafast frequency activities, as shown previously. 1 , 7 This study aimed to analyze resting‐state iEEG data from intrahippocampal hybrid (macro/micro) depth electrodes in a cohort of patients with epilepsy using high sampling frequencies (25, 30, or 32 kHz). Here, we focused on EEG activities between 2 and 8 kHz. Hypothetical ultrafast electrical events within the human brain might bear distinct functional significance when compared to lower frequencies and possibly could substantially contribute to better insight into the pathophysiology of epileptic disorders on the microscopic level.

**Document:** Components of generalized onset seizures with focal evolution progressing to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures using quantitative electroencephalography in children: Focal or generalized?
**Section:** INTRODUCTION

Idiopathic generalized epilepsy (IGE) is an epileptic syndrome representing 15%–20% of people with epilepsy (a subtype of genetic generalized epilepsy [GGE]), encompassing childhood absence epilepsy, juvenile absence epilepsy (JAE), juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME), and generalized tonic–clonic seizures alone. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 GGE accounts for 23%–43% of new onset epilepsy in children and adolescents. 5 , 6 , 7 The mean age at onset varies depending of combination of absence, myoclonic, myoclonic–tonic–clonic and generalized tonic–clonic (GTC). 7 These types of seizures may present forced head and eyes deviation or version. 3 , 7 , 8 Eighty percent of them respond to the appropriate treatment. 9 The electroencephalogram (EEG) typically shows 2.5–5.5‐Hz generalized spike–wave (GSW)/generalized polyspike–wave (GPSW) elicited by hyperventilation, sleep, or awakening with or without photoparoxysmal response and may have fragmentation. 8 , 10 , 11 , 12 Absence seizures progressing to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures were reported as “the double generalization phenomenon in juvenile absence epilepsy” 13 or “absence‐to‐bilateral‐tonic‐clonic seizure as a generalized seizure type.” 14 Some of these patients may have focal features during the progression to a GTC seizure, a phenomenon referred to as generalized onset seizures with focal evolution (GOFE), 15 which was first described in 2009 by Williamson. 16 The incidence and prevalence of this seizure type is unknown. Continuous video‐EEG monitoring is the gold standard diagnostic tool. Quantitative EEG (QEEG) processes, transforms, and analyzes the digital EEG signals using complex mathematical algorithms, giving information about specific frequency bands, signal complexity, simplistic analysis of connectivity, and network analysis. 17 , 18 Following the International League Against Epilepsy seizure classification and QEEG analysis, we hypothesize that absence seizures may lead to focal evolution before progressing to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures. The primary objective of this study was to characterize the electrographic abnormalities and possible network underlying this transition from an absence to a bilateral tonic–clonic seizure in patients with generalized epilepsy.

**Document:** Paroxysmal slow waves mark ictal networks.

question: What information does electroencephalography contribute to epilepsy evaluation?
answer:
### Main Topic: Electroencephalography in Epilepsy Evaluation

Electroencephalography (EEG) significantly contributes to epilepsy evaluation by providing crucial information on seizure activity, seizure focus, and underlying brain function.

#### Core Clinical Concepts:

• **Interictal Abnormalities:** EEG can detect interictal abnormalities, which are abnormal electrical patterns present between seizures. These abnormalities can indicate the presence of an epileptogenic zone, helping to localize the seizure focus. For instance, focal spikes or sharp waves in the interictal EEG can suggest a focal seizure onset zone. The presence and characteristics of these abnormalities can guide further diagnostic and therapeutic decisions.

• **Ictal Patterns:** During seizures, EEG can capture ictal patterns, which are abnormal electrical discharges that occur during seizure activity. These patterns can provide valuable information on seizure semiology, including seizure type, duration, and spread. For example, a seizure that begins with a focal discharge and then generalizes can indicate a focal seizure onset with secondary generalization. The ictal EEG can also help identify seizure-related changes in consciousness, motor activity, or other clinical features.

• **Background Activity:** EEG can assess background activity, which reflects the normal electrical function of the brain. Abnormal background activity, such as slow-wave activity or diffuse slowing, can indicate underlying brain dysfunction or structural abnormalities. This information can be particularly useful in patients with refractory epilepsy or those undergoing surgical evaluation.

• **Spectral Analysis:** Advanced EEG techniques, such as spectral analysis, can provide quantitative measures of brain activity. These measures can help identify changes in brain function associated with epilepsy, including alterations in power spectral density, coherence, or phase-locking values. Spectral analysis can also aid in the identification of seizure-related changes in brain activity.

• **EEG-MRI Correlation:** Combining EEG with MRI can enhance diagnostic accuracy and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying pathology. EEG-MRI correlation can help identify structural abnormalities, such as hippocampal sclerosis or cortical dysplasia, that may be associated with seizure activity.

• **Long-Term Monitoring:** Long-term EEG monitoring, often using video-EEG or ambulatory EEG, can capture seizures that occur infrequently or during sleep. This information can be invaluable in patients with rare or nocturnal seizures, helping to identify seizure triggers and optimize treatment.

• **Response to Treatment:** EEG can also be used to monitor the response to antiepileptic medication or other treatments. Changes in interictal or ictal patterns can indicate treatment efficacy or the need for medication adjustments.

• **Surgical Evaluation:** In patients undergoing surgical evaluation for epilepsy, EEG can provide critical information on seizure focus, lateralization, and the extent of epileptogenic tissue. This information can help guide surgical planning and optimize outcomes.

In summary, EEG is a fundamental tool in epilepsy evaluation, providing a wealth of information on seizure activity, seizure focus, and underlying brain function. By combining EEG with other diagnostic modalities, such as MRI and clinical evaluation, clinicians can develop a comprehensive understanding of the patient's epilepsy and optimize treatment strategies.

question: How can focal and generalized seizures differ?
answer:
### Main Topic: Differentiation of Focal and Generalized Seizures

Focal seizures originate within networks limited to one hemisphere and may be discretely localized or more widely distributed, whereas generalized seizures arise from and rapidly engage bilaterally distributed networks from the onset. The fundamental distinction lies in the anatomical extent of the initial ictal discharge and the subsequent recruitment of cortical and subcortical structures.

#### Core Clinical Concepts:

• **Anatomical Origin and Network Involvement:** Focal seizures are characterized by an onset within a specific neural network, often restricted to one hemisphere. These may remain localized (focal aware) or spread to involve broader cortical areas (focal impaired awareness). In contrast, generalized seizures involve both hemispheres simultaneously from the point of origin. This implies that the underlying pathophysiology of generalized seizures involves a rapid, synchronous discharge across the thalamocortical loops, which act as a pacemaker for the entire brain, rather than a localized cortical focus.

• **Clinical Semiology and Consciousness:** The clinical presentation of focal seizures is highly dependent on the specific cortical region involved (e.g., motor cortex, temporal lobe, occipital lobe). If the seizure remains focal and the patient retains awareness, it is classified as focal aware; if awareness is impaired, it is focal impaired awareness. Generalized seizures, by definition, involve a loss of consciousness or awareness from the onset, as the bilateral network engagement disrupts the ascending reticular activating system and thalamocortical integration necessary for maintaining a conscious state.

• **Electroencephalographic (EEG) Patterns:** The diagnostic hallmark of a focal seizure is a localized ictal discharge, such as spikes, sharp waves, or rhythmic activity confined to a specific electrode region (e.g., temporal or frontal leads). Generalized seizures are characterized by bilateral, synchronous, and symmetric discharges across all leads. Common patterns include 3 Hz spike-and-wave complexes in absence seizures or generalized polyspike-and-wave discharges in tonic-clonic seizures, reflecting the widespread, simultaneous recruitment of cortical neurons.

• **Etiological Considerations:** Focal seizures are frequently associated with structural brain abnormalities, such as cortical dysplasia, hippocampal sclerosis, tumors, or prior ischemic injury (lesional epilepsy). Generalized seizures are more commonly associated with genetic or idiopathic epilepsy syndromes, where the underlying mechanism involves channelopathies or polygenic predispositions that lower the seizure threshold across the entire brain. However, it is critical to note that focal seizures can evolve into bilateral tonic-clonic seizures (focal to bilateral tonic-clonic), which must be distinguished from primary generalized seizures to ensure appropriate diagnostic workup and treatment.

• **Management and Pharmacological Principles:** The choice of anti-seizure medication (ASM) is heavily influenced by the seizure classification. Focal seizures are typically managed with narrow-spectrum ASMs (e.g., carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, or lacosamide) that stabilize neuronal membranes and inhibit voltage-gated sodium channels. Generalized seizures often require broad-spectrum ASMs (e.g., valproate, levetiracetam, or lamotrigine) that modulate thalamocortical circuitry or enhance inhibitory GABAergic transmission. Using a narrow-spectrum sodium channel blocker for certain generalized epilepsy syndromes (such as absence or myoclonic epilepsy) can paradoxically exacerbate the seizure frequency, highlighting the clinical necessity of accurate classification.

question: How can focal and generalized seizures differ?
answer:
### Main Topic: Differentiation of Focal and Generalized Seizures

Focal seizures originate within neural networks limited to one cerebral hemisphere, whereas generalized seizures arise from and rapidly engage bilaterally distributed networks from the onset [S1, S4, S8]. While these categories are distinct in their anatomical initiation, clinical and electrographic features can occasionally overlap, such as in "generalized onset seizures with focal evolution" (GOFE), which can complicate diagnostic classification [S2, S3].

#### Supporting Clinical Evidence:

• **Anatomical and Network Distinctions:** Focal seizures are defined by an onset restricted to a specific network within one hemisphere, which may manifest as focal aware or focal impaired awareness seizures [S1, S8]. Conversely, generalized seizures involve bilateral cortical and subcortical networks from the start, typically presenting as absence, myoclonic, atonic, or generalized tonic-clonic seizures [S1].

• **Electrographic Patterns:** Focal epilepsy is characterized by epileptiform activity confined to a single hemisphere on EEG [S4]. In contrast, generalized epilepsy typically displays generalized spike-wave (GSW) or polyspike-wave (GPSW) activity [S3, S4]. However, quantitative EEG (QEEG) analysis has revealed that some generalized seizures may exhibit focal electroclinical features during their progression, a phenomenon known as GOFE, which can lead to diagnostic dilemmas and potential misclassification [S2, S3, S5].

• **Clinical Implications of Misclassification:** Accurate differentiation is critical for therapeutic selection, as the inappropriate use of narrow-spectrum antiseizure medications in patients with generalized epilepsy can be ineffective or potentially exacerbate certain seizure types [S2]. For instance, generalized epilepsy syndromes often require broad-spectrum agents like valproic acid or lamotrigine, whereas focal epilepsy management focuses on different pharmacological strategies and, in refractory cases, potential surgical intervention [S2, S4, S8].

• **Diagnostic Challenges:** Because seizure semiology—such as head deviation, automatisms, or postictal confusion—can be present in both focal and generalized types, clinicians rely on a combination of detailed patient history, neuroimaging (e.g., MRI), and continuous video-EEG monitoring to establish an accurate diagnosis [S4, S5, S7].

### [Layer 3 > Epilepsy > DISCUSSION > Components of generalized onset seizures with focal evolution progressing to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures using quantitative electroencephalography in children: Focal or generalized?]
**Document:** Components of generalized onset seizures with focal evolution progressing to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures using quantitative electroencephalography in children: Focal or generalized?
**Section:** DISCUSSION

GOFE is an electroclinical pattern in which generalized onset epileptic activity, manifesting as an absence seizure, evolves into focal discharges during the same ictal event, often followed by bilateral tonic–clonic activity. This electroclinical pattern has been described in patients with GGE. In a group of patients with GGE, the distinction between generalized and focal epileptiform activity can be blurred, with features that fall in between these two extremes, and in some cases, there may be an overlap. 15 , 16 , 19 These seizure patterns pose a diagnostic dilemma and are a challenge for even the most experienced epileptologists. The cohort of patients with GOFE studied in our institution were all females; this is a meaningful finding. We have no explanation for this, however, including our cases, 60% are females, 28% males, and 12% unknown (see Table S2). More work is needed to determine why females may be more at risk of this pattern. Clinically and electrographically, our patients showed features similar to those reported in the first description of this seizure type (2009), which included six patients with IGE showing generalized onset seizures with focal EEG and clinical evolution. 16 Another study in Nashville (2016) reported nine patients with generalized epilepsy who showed semiology concerning for focal seizures, with video‐EEG monitoring confirming GOFE. 19 Recently, GOFE was reported in three patients in Strasbourg (2022), highlighting that GOFE shares many features with GGE and that its recognition is clinically important to avoid misdiagnosis of focal epilepsy and consequently the inappropriate use of narrow spectrum antiseizure medications. 20 Recently, another study reported that focal electroclinical features are commonly seen in generalized seizures, whereas GOFE represents a largely unknown ictal variation in GGE, bearing a risk of misclassification (see Table S2). 21 In some cases, the prominent focal signs could lead to intensive video‐EEG monitoring as part of a presurgical evaluation even including stereo‐EEG. 15 , 19 , 22 Recognizing this seizure type implies treatment reassessment including the use of broad spectrum antiseizure medication such as valproic acid alone or in association with lamotrigine. 22 Additionally, some specific single gene genetic conditions as SLC13A5 have different seizure types, including absence seizures with the main electrographic patterns including 3‐Hz generalized spike and wave showing features of IGE. 23 Three theories were proposed to explain this seizure type. 24 The first is focal cerebral dysfunction or a focal/lateralized weakness of seizure initiation–termination mechanisms. 16 The second is a focal ictal transformation of an IGE seizure variant due to a coexistent focal epilepsy (not seizures), which may require more complex management. 24 The third proposes that existing hyperexcitable cortical areas or systems may continue firing independently after the diffuse/generalized corticothalamic oscillations are inhibited. 25 Furthermore, a review of generalized absence seizures described the presence of different motor clinical manifestations, even with the same electrographic pattern, which could be related to the broad neuronal network involved in the seizure generation and seizure propagation, implying thalamocortical fibers. 26 This statement is reinforced by functional brain MRI studies,

The second is a focal ictal transformation of an IGE seizure variant due to a coexistent focal epilepsy (not seizures), which may require more complex management. 24 The third proposes that existing hyperexcitable cortical areas or systems may continue firing independently after the diffuse/generalized corticothalamic oscillations are inhibited. 25 Furthermore, a review of generalized absence seizures described the presence of different motor clinical manifestations, even with the same electrographic pattern, which could be related to the broad neuronal network involved in the seizure generation and seizure propagation, implying thalamocortical fibers. 26 This statement is reinforced by functional brain MRI studies, which reported the involvement of the thalamus, caudate nuclei, and default mode areas during generalized spike–wave paroxysms and absence seizures. Moreover, they confirm high synchronization activity in the thalamocortical network by demonstration of blood oxygen level‐dependent (BOLD) activation in the thalamus, the frontomesial cortex, and the cerebellum, and BOLD deactivation in default mode areas. 27 , 28 In our cohort of patient, we found a considerable right‐lateralized frontal predominance. Woermann et al. analyzed a voxel‐based morphometry of 35 patients with IGE, reporting subtle changes in the frontal lobe by MRI. 29 Seneviratne et al. reported volume reduction or increase in the frontal and thalamic cortical areas in a voxel‐based morphometry study. 28 Kim et al. reported small volume of cortical gray matter in the right frontal lobe as well as regional smaller volume in the rostral and middle frontal, right lateral orbitofrontal, right precentral, right superior and middle temporal regions. Also, small volume was noticed in the left middle and inferior temporal regions. 30 The reason the right frontal lobe has more predisposition or impairment in patients with IGE remains unclear. Is there an anatomical predisposition or is this a consequence of the continuous thalamocortical network activation? Deep evaluation of the seizures with QEEG analysis, specifically using the spectrogram, increases the accuracy of the diagnosis in different seizure types due to sensitivity of 72% to identify seizures and sensitivity of 94% to determine focality of the seizures. 18 QEEG analysis with Persyst software uses deep learning and artificial neuronal networks to identify and classify interictal and ictal epileptiform discharges. Spike detection and seizure detection views are the most accurate tools to monitor background activity, screen for artifacts, analyze waveform morphology, and map voltage field spread. 18 One study investigated under QEEG structured data segmentation including frequency bands, cortical regions, and hemispheric localization for the accurate diagnosis of pediatric epilepsy. 31 In our cohort, the analysis described was applied and confirmed our diagnosis of GOFE. The presence of the green bar (spike detection generalized) time lock with absence seizure suddenly stopped and led to focal evolution in the red bar (right hemisphere) or blue bar (left hemisphere) to bilateral tonic–clonic seizure (red bar in seizure probability and black bars in spike detection in all foci; Figure 1). Subsequently, we confidently halted any further evaluation.

### [Layer 3 > Epilepsy > INTRODUCTION > Components of generalized onset seizures with focal evolution progressing to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures using quantitative electroencephalography in children: Focal or generalized?]
**Document:** Components of generalized onset seizures with focal evolution progressing to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures using quantitative electroencephalography in children: Focal or generalized?
**Section:** INTRODUCTION

Idiopathic generalized epilepsy (IGE) is an epileptic syndrome representing 15%–20% of people with epilepsy (a subtype of genetic generalized epilepsy [GGE]), encompassing childhood absence epilepsy, juvenile absence epilepsy (JAE), juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME), and generalized tonic–clonic seizures alone. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 GGE accounts for 23%–43% of new onset epilepsy in children and adolescents. 5 , 6 , 7 The mean age at onset varies depending of combination of absence, myoclonic, myoclonic–tonic–clonic and generalized tonic–clonic (GTC). 7 These types of seizures may present forced head and eyes deviation or version. 3 , 7 , 8 Eighty percent of them respond to the appropriate treatment. 9 The electroencephalogram (EEG) typically shows 2.5–5.5‐Hz generalized spike–wave (GSW)/generalized polyspike–wave (GPSW) elicited by hyperventilation, sleep, or awakening with or without photoparoxysmal response and may have fragmentation. 8 , 10 , 11 , 12 Absence seizures progressing to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures were reported as “the double generalization phenomenon in juvenile absence epilepsy” 13 or “absence‐to‐bilateral‐tonic‐clonic seizure as a generalized seizure type.” 14 Some of these patients may have focal features during the progression to a GTC seizure, a phenomenon referred to as generalized onset seizures with focal evolution (GOFE), 15 which was first described in 2009 by Williamson. 16 The incidence and prevalence of this seizure type is unknown. Continuous video‐EEG monitoring is the gold standard diagnostic tool. Quantitative EEG (QEEG) processes, transforms, and analyzes the digital EEG signals using complex mathematical algorithms, giving information about specific frequency bands, signal complexity, simplistic analysis of connectivity, and network analysis. 17 , 18 Following the International League Against Epilepsy seizure classification and QEEG analysis, we hypothesize that absence seizures may lead to focal evolution before progressing to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures. The primary objective of this study was to characterize the electrographic abnormalities and possible network underlying this transition from an absence to a bilateral tonic–clonic seizure in patients with generalized epilepsy.

### [Layer 3 > Epilepsy > Introduction > Stem cell-based therapeutics in epilepsy: current advances and future prospects.]
**Document:** Stem cell-based therapeutics in epilepsy: current advances and future prospects.
**Section:** Introduction

Epilepsy is a common neurological disorder with a global prevalence of approximately 600 per 100 000, affecting more than 50 million individuals worldwide.1,2 Seizures occur from abnormal synchronous neuronal firing involving focal or diffuse cortical networks, triggered by structural, infectious, or metabolic perturbations. Epilepsy manifests as a complex disorder with environmental effects acting on inherited susceptibility, mediated by common variation in particular genes, rather than a single mutation or cause.1 Diverse causes of epilepsy result in a bimodal distribution, with genetic causes in childhood and accumulated injury to the brain (eg, trauma, tumors) in the elderly.2 As epilepsy displays a wide range of possible pathophysiological features, from well-recognized convulsions to psychological symptoms, a detailed history serves as the cornerstone of the diagnosis.1 Additional tests such as electroencephalogram (EEG) and neuroimaging, preferably magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), help identify the structural and functional causes, facilitating diagnosis and classification of epilepsy.3,4 The International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) defines epilepsy by any of the following conditions: (1) At least two unprovoked seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart; (2) one unprovoked seizure and a probability of further seizures at least 60% (ie, comparable to recurrent risk after two unprovoked seizures) over the next 10 years; (3) diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome.5 Epilepsy is classified into four main classes: Focal, Generalized, Combined, and Unknown.6 Patients with generalized epilepsy exhibit generalized spike-wave activity on EEG, whereas focal epilepsy shows epileptiform activity that is confined to a single hemisphere. The combined epilepsy, such as Dravet syndrome and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, is defined by both generalized spike-wave and focal epileptiform discharges during seizure. Lastly, the unknown group refers to cases where epilepsy is confirmed but the type cannot be determined due to insufficient information, such as an unavailable or uninformative EEG. Noteworthy, epilepsy may involve multiple seizure types in the same patient. Progress in genomic technology is exposing the complex genetic architecture of the common types of epilepsy, facilitating more precise classification and treatment design.1,7 Epilepsy greatly reduces quality of life and poses a risk of a sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP).7 Current antiseizure medications (ASMs) depend on inhibition of sodium channel or calcium channel, enhancement of gamma-aminobutyric acid-related (GABAergic) inhibition, and glutamate-mediated excitation blockage.7 However, ASMs are effective in 60%-70% of individuals and only suppress seizures but not the underlying epileptogenesis, resulting in an unchanged long-term prognosis.7 Apart from frequent adverse effects that limit tolerance, and thus, the efficacy of ASMs, approximately 30% of epileptic patients are resistant to treatment despite accurate diagnosis and carefully monitored drug levels.7 Epilepsy surgery appears as the most effective way to achieve long-term seizure remission, up to 30%-60%, for patients with focal epilepsy refractory to medications.1 Nonetheless, epilepsy surgery remains significantly underutilized due to the requirement for extensive evaluations and specialized expertise.8 Consequently, many novel treatments have emerged in the past decades, aiming to suppress underlying epileptogenesis and restore damaged neural circuits.

Seizures result from paroxysmal, excessive, hypersynchronous electrical discharges of aggregate cerebral cortical neurons. Pathophysiologic mechanisms include an imbalance between glutamate-mediated excitatory neurotransmission and GABA-mediated inhibitory neurotransmission, altered voltage-gated ion channels, and abnormal neural circuit plasticity. ### [Layer 3 > Epilepsy > SANAD II RCT > SANAD II: Levetiracetam vs Lamotrigine in Newly Diagnosed Focal Epilepsy (RCT)]
**Document:** SANAD II: Levetiracetam vs Lamotrigine in Newly Diagnosed Focal Epilepsy (RCT)
**Section:** Introduction

Epilepsy is a common condition with a prevalence of 0·5–1% and lifetime incidence of up to 5%.1, 2 Epilepsy is a complex disorder with many seizure types and causes. It is uniquely stigmatising and negatively affects quality of life (QOL), education, and employment prospects.3, 4 Anti-seizure medications are the mainstay of treatment and approximately 70% of people with epilepsy will achieve a remission from seizures, half of whom may be able to stop treatment without a seizure recurrence. Around two-thirds of people with epilepsy have focal epilepsy; seizures that start in a neuronal network limited to one cerebral hemisphere. Seizure types include focal aware seizures (previously called simple partial seizures), focal seizures with impaired awareness (previously called complex partial seizures), and focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures (previously called secondarily generalised tonic clonic seizures).5, 6, 7 Focal epilepsy can start at any age, and the incidence distribution is U shaped, with higher incidence in young and elderly people. Because of ageing populations, in many countries the incidence of focal epilepsy is higher in older people than in younger people.2 Although focal epilepsies can be classified according to site of seizure onset and cause, there is no evidence to suggest that one syndrome or cause responds better to one specific treatment than to another.8 The drug management is therefore generally similar whatever the cause or syndrome. Guidelines typically recommend lamotrigine or carbamazepine as first-line treatment,9 in part informed by the first standard and new antiepileptic drug trial (SANAD I),10 which identified lamotrigine as non-inferior to carbamazepine for time to 12-month remission and superior to carbamazepine, gabapentin, oxcarbazepine, and topiramate for time to treatment failure. Since the publication of SANAD I, several newer treatments have become available, including levetiracetam and zonisamide. Levetiracetam is a commonly prescribed anti-seizure medication with evidence of efficacy as monotherapy in patients with focal epilepsy based on finding non-inferiority compared with carbamazepine for 6-month seizure remission and similar tolerability in a regulatory trial11 that did not assess longer term effectiveness. A second open-label trial12 compared levetiracetam with physicians' choice of carbamazepine or valproate, and it showed no significant difference between carbamazepine and levetiracetam for time to first seizure and time to treatment failure. However, that trial12 had a maximum follow-up of 12 months and therefore could not assess longer term outcomes needed to inform policy. In the 2012 NICE epilepsy guideline,9 levetiracetam was not recommended as a first-line treatment on the basis of an analysis indicating that it was not cost-effective. However, levetiracetam has since become available in generic form and is widely prescribed. Zonisamide has been available for many years in Japan13 and southeast Asia. Its licence for use as a monotherapy is also based on a regulatory study14 showing non-inferiority to carbamazepine for 6-month seizure remission rates. The longer term comparative clinical and cost-effectiveness of zonisamide is unknown. The aim of SANAD II was to assess the longer term clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of levetiracetam and zonisamide compared with lamotrigine in people with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy.
