Stress is one of the most commonly reported seizure triggers. 5 , 6 Beyond everyday stressors, people with epilepsy may face additional burdens, including medication side effects, driving restrictions, workplace limitations, financial strain, relationship challenges, and stigma. 7 , 8 Recently, there has been growing interest in lifestyle modifications and their potential impact on seizure frequency, QOL, cognition, and mental health. 9 , 10 , 11 These interventions encompass a wide range of strategies, including dietary approaches, physical activity, mind–body practices, and behavioral therapies, and likely act through multiple mechanisms. Whereas stress reduction may contribute to the effects of some interventions, others may influence seizure susceptibility through biological, physiological, or neurochemical pathways, highlighting the importance of evaluating these approaches collectively and systematically. Lifestyle medicine (LM)—a nonpharmacological specialty using interventions such as nutrition, exercise, stress reduction, and sleep to prevent or treat chronic diseases 12 , 13 —has shown benefits for general health and in reducing anxiety, depression, and stress. 14 , 15 Although its application in epilepsy has been limited to small studies and case reports, early findings suggest LM may help reduce seizures when used alongside standard treatments, likely through its stress‐reducing and health‐promoting effects. Several systematic reviews have examined LM interventions in epilepsy, including yoga, 16 mindfulness‐based therapies, 17 music interventions, 18 , 19 dietary therapies such as ketogenic and modified Atkins diets, 20 , 21 psychosocial and behavioral therapies, 10 , 22 and exercise. 23 Although these reviews suggest potential benefits of each individual type of intervention, their findings are difficult to compare because of nonuniform outcomes and heterogeneous study designs. Comparing the effectiveness of different LMs is crucial from a practical standpoint; although nonpharmacological interventions are generally appealing as a whole, there is a lack of an evidence‐based framework for prioritizing LM selection and introduction based on patient preference and accessibility. To address this gap, we conducted the first comprehensive systematic review and meta‐analysis to quantitatively compare the effectiveness of diverse LM interventions for seizure reduction. By integrating prospective and randomized trials across modalities, our study provides a unified estimate of efficacy, identifies understudied approaches, and outlines priorities for future LM research. These results offer a practical reference for clinicians seeking to individualize LM recommendations in epilepsy care.

### [Layer 3 > Epilepsy > INTRODUCTION > Long-term prognosis of pharmacotherapy in newly diagnosed focal epilepsy patients and the predictive value of baseline seizure timing: A prospective cohort study.]
**Document:** Long-term prognosis of pharmacotherapy in newly diagnosed focal epilepsy patients and the predictive value of baseline seizure timing: A prospective cohort study.
**Section:** INTRODUCTION

Epilepsy is a disorder with multiple etiologies, including genetic and structural causes, that affects more than 50 million people worldwide. 1 Among these, focal seizures are the most common type, accounting for 61% of all epilepsy patients. 2 Antiseizure medications (ASMs) represent the mainstay of treatment, with approximately two thirds of patients achieving long‐term remission after ASM initiation, whereas one third progress to drug‐resistant epilepsy (DRE). 3 , 4 The course of epilepsy is dynamically variable, with seizure control status influenced by time, therapeutic interventions, and baseline characteristics; some patients may even alternate between drug‐responsive and drug‐resistant states. 5 Prolonged follow‐up periods are therefore critical for distinguishing persistent remission from unstable fluctuating disease courses. 6 , 7 Clarifying the factors affecting long‐term prognosis and developing targeted interventions is thus of great significance for optimizing clinical epilepsy management. Previous studies have identified multiple independent prognostic predictors for epilepsy, including abnormal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings, epileptiform electroencephalographic (EEG) discharges, and other clinical factors. 8 , 9 , 10 In recent years, the impact of sleep‐related factors on epilepsy prognosis has gradually gained attention, but existing research has mostly been limited to early outcomes or first seizures. 11 , 12 No study has systematically explored the associations between baseline seizure timing and drug responsiveness. Given the complex interaction between sleep and epilepsy, this prospective cohort study aimed to determine the long‐term prognosis of newly diagnosed focal epilepsy patients receiving standardized ASM therapy, and to clarify whether baseline seizure timing serves as an independent prognostic factor for this population.

### [Layer 3 > Epilepsy > INTRODUCTION > Information needs of patients considering epilepsy surgery: A scoping review.]
**Document:** Information needs of patients considering epilepsy surgery: A scoping review.
**Section:** INTRODUCTION

Epilepsy can have profound impacts on an individual's life, with increased risk of premature mortality, poor mental health outcomes, and decreased quality of life. For most people, antiseizure medications can control seizure occurrence, mitigating negative impacts of epilepsy on life expectancy and quality of life. However, one third of people with epilepsy will be drug‐resistant, meaning they will continue to have seizures despite two adequate trials of different antiseizure medications. 1 For patients with drug‐resistant epilepsy, surgery has been shown to promote seizure remission, reduce associated mortality and morbidity, and improve quality of life. 2 , 3 , 4 Increased success of seizure‐free status postsurgery is associated with earlier referrals after diagnosis of drug‐resistance is established. 5 Current guidelines suggest that surgery should be considered as a treatment in these cases, but despite positive outcomes, surgery remains underutilized. 6 The underutilization of epilepsy surgery has been attributed to a variety of reasons, including patient fears regarding surgery risks and a lack of high‐quality resources to inform and guide patients and their caregivers in making these decisions. Interest in epilepsy surgery has been shown to change when additional information on benefits and complications is provided, reinforcing the role of patient education in decision‐making. 7 , 8 Because misconceptions about the risk of surgery are prominent, 9 it is important that information shared with people living with epilepsy is accurate and informed by their needs. Information resources that focus on epilepsy surgery are highly variable in the content provided, readability, and information quality and often fail to address the specific needs of this patient population. To address the above gaps, the primary aim of this study was to conduct a scoping review to identify the information needs of people considering epilepsy surgery. This includes the specific type of information content, timing and delivery of information, and quality of information desired by patients, caregivers, and family members. Our secondary aims were to identify the barriers and facilitators that exist in deciding to undergo epilepsy surgery and establish what elements are needed when creating a resource to support patient decision‐making about epilepsy surgery. Findings from this scoping review could inform the future development of high‐quality resources that could help patients and their care partners with epilepsy surgery decision‐making.

### [Layer 3 > Epilepsy > SANAD II RCT > SANAD II: Levetiracetam vs Lamotrigine in Newly Diagnosed Focal Epilepsy (RCT)]
**Document:** SANAD II: Levetiracetam vs Lamotrigine in Newly Diagnosed Focal Epilepsy (RCT)
**Section:** Introduction

Epilepsy is a common condition with a prevalence of 0·5–1% and lifetime incidence of up to 5%.1, 2 Epilepsy is a complex disorder with many seizure types and causes. It is uniquely stigmatising and negatively affects quality of life (QOL), education, and employment prospects.3, 4 Anti-seizure medications are the mainstay of treatment and approximately 70% of people with epilepsy will achieve a remission from seizures, half of whom may be able to stop treatment without a seizure recurrence. Around two-thirds of people with epilepsy have focal epilepsy; seizures that start in a neuronal network limited to one cerebral hemisphere. Seizure types include focal aware seizures (previously called simple partial seizures), focal seizures with impaired awareness (previously called complex partial seizures), and focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures (previously called secondarily generalised tonic clonic seizures).5, 6, 7 Focal epilepsy can start at any age, and the incidence distribution is U shaped, with higher incidence in young and elderly people. Because of ageing populations, in many countries the incidence of focal epilepsy is higher in older people than in younger people.2 Although focal epilepsies can be classified according to site of seizure onset and cause, there is no evidence to suggest that one syndrome or cause responds better to one specific treatment than to another.8 The drug management is therefore generally similar whatever the cause or syndrome. Guidelines typically recommend lamotrigine or carbamazepine as first-line treatment,9 in part informed by the first standard and new antiepileptic drug trial (SANAD I),10 which identified lamotrigine as non-inferior to carbamazepine for time to 12-month remission and superior to carbamazepine, gabapentin, oxcarbazepine, and topiramate for time to treatment failure. Since the publication of SANAD I, several newer treatments have become available, including levetiracetam and zonisamide. Levetiracetam is a commonly prescribed anti-seizure medication with evidence of efficacy as monotherapy in patients with focal epilepsy based on finding non-inferiority compared with carbamazepine for 6-month seizure remission and similar tolerability in a regulatory trial11 that did not assess longer term effectiveness. A second open-label trial12 compared levetiracetam with physicians' choice of carbamazepine or valproate, and it showed no significant difference between carbamazepine and levetiracetam for time to first seizure and time to treatment failure. However, that trial12 had a maximum follow-up of 12 months and therefore could not assess longer term outcomes needed to inform policy. In the 2012 NICE epilepsy guideline,9 levetiracetam was not recommended as a first-line treatment on the basis of an analysis indicating that it was not cost-effective. However, levetiracetam has since become available in generic form and is widely prescribed. Zonisamide has been available for many years in Japan13 and southeast Asia. Its licence for use as a monotherapy is also based on a regulatory study14 showing non-inferiority to carbamazepine for 6-month seizure remission rates. The longer term comparative clinical and cost-effectiveness of zonisamide is unknown. The aim of SANAD II was to assess the longer term clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of levetiracetam and zonisamide compared with lamotrigine in people with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy.

### [Layer 3 > Epilepsy > Introduction > Akkermansia muciniphila enhances washed microbiota transplantation in the treatment of epilepsy.]
**Document:** Akkermansia muciniphila enhances washed microbiota transplantation in the treatment of epilepsy.
**Section:** Introduction

Epilepsy is a chronic and debilitating neurological disorder with a threefold higher risk of mortality and disability compared to the general population. It is characterized by recurrent, unprovoked spontaneous seizures. Although anti-epileptic drugs are the first-line treatment, they achieve full seizure control in only approximately 70% of patients. This implies that roughly one-third of patients experience refractory seizures, enduring persistent seizures. Despite advanced interventions such as surgery and neurostimulation, a subset of patients remains unresponsive, highlighting the urgent need for more effective and safer therapeutic strategies. Accumulating evidence from animal and clinical studies suggests a link between gut microbiota dysbiosis and the pathophysiology of epilepsy. Approaches that target the microbiota–gut–brain axis, including ketogenic diets, probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, and antibiotics, have shown promise in seizure reduction. Notably, a ketogenic diet has been reported to lessen seizure frequency of refractory epilepsy. Nonetheless, the impact of probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, and antibiotics on seizures remains inconclusive, with mixed results from limited studies. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is a potent treatment for reconstructing the composition and function of the gut microbiota, showing promising therapeutic value in the treatment of dysbiosis-related diseases. In 2015, our team made a serendipitous clinical discovery that FMT cured a 17-year history of epilepsy in a girl with Crohn’s disease. Inspired by this finding, we launched the present trial to evaluate the efficacy of FMT in epilepsy. A new method of FMT utilizing the automatic purification machine and the washing process was named as washed microbiota transplantation (WMT). The WMT procedure decreases over 73% of the FMT-related fever compared with the manual FMT procedure. We recently reported that WMT from healthy donors significantly alleviated distal symmetric polyneuropathy in a randomized cohort of 22 patients with diabetes mellitus. Moreover, FMT appears to be beneficial for several other neurological and psychiatric conditions, including autism spectrum disorder, depression, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. However, the efficacy of microbiota transplantation varies significantly across different diseases. Then we introduced a new therapeutic concept, X-augmented washed microbiota transplantation (X-auWMT), which combines a disease-specific beneficial microbe “X” with WMT to enhance its effectiveness. We simultaneously initiated two prospective studies, one focusing on radiation enteritis and the present study on epilepsy, to validate the concept of X-auWMT. Recently, we have reported the Holdemanella biformis-auWMT in the treatment of radiation enteritis, and here we report the application of the X-auWMT concept to epilepsy treatment. Our integrated clinical and microbial analysis revealed that the clinical response to WMT was associated with a significant increase in Akkermansia muciniphila (A. muciniphila). We designed complementary experiments in a mouse model of epilepsy, aiming to elucidate the mechanistic role of A. muciniphila-augmented WMT (Am-auWMT).

question: How does chronic heart failure alter cardiac output?
answer:
### Main Topic: Chronic Heart Failure and Cardiac Output

Chronic heart failure (CHF) leads to a reduction in cardiac output (CO) due to impaired cardiac function, resulting in decreased stroke volume (SV) and increased systemic vascular resistance (SVR).

#### Core Clinical Concepts:

• **Cardiac Remodeling:** CHF leads to cardiac remodeling, characterized by hypertrophy and fibrosis of the myocardium. This remodeling process impairs the heart's ability to contract and relax, reducing SV and ultimately CO. The increased wall thickness and stiffness of the ventricle increase the afterload, further reducing SV and CO.

• **Decreased Contractility:** The failing heart exhibits decreased contractility, which is often referred to as systolic dysfunction. This is due to the loss of functional myocytes, decreased expression of contractile proteins, and altered calcium handling. The reduced contractility impairs the heart's ability to generate force and pump blood effectively, leading to decreased SV and CO.

• **Increased Systemic Vascular Resistance:** CHF leads to increased SVR, which is a result of the activation of the sympathetic nervous system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). The increased SVR increases the afterload, further reducing SV and CO. The increased SVR also leads to increased peripheral resistance, which can further compromise cardiac output.

• **Decreased Cardiac Preload:** CHF often leads to decreased cardiac preload, which is the volume of blood in the ventricle at the end of diastole. The decreased preload reduces the stroke volume, as the ventricle is not able to fill with enough blood to generate an adequate stroke volume.

• **Compensatory Mechanisms:** The body attempts to compensate for the reduced CO by increasing heart rate and contractility. However, these compensatory mechanisms are often inadequate and can lead to further cardiac remodeling and dysfunction.

• **Clinical Presentation:** Patients with CHF often present with symptoms such as fatigue, shortness of breath, and peripheral edema. The clinical presentation can vary depending on the underlying cause of the CHF and the severity of the disease.

• **Diagnostic Criteria:** The diagnosis of CHF is typically made based on a combination of clinical presentation, physical examination, and diagnostic tests such as echocardiography and cardiac biomarkers. The diagnostic criteria for CHF include symptoms of heart failure, evidence of structural heart disease, and decreased cardiac function.

• **Management Principles:** The management of CHF involves a combination of pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions. The primary goal of treatment is to reduce symptoms, improve quality of life, and reduce morbidity and mortality. Pharmacological interventions include ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, and diuretics, while non-pharmacological interventions include lifestyle modifications and device therapy.

• **Pharmacological Classes:** The pharmacological management of CHF involves the use of several classes of medications, including:

   • ACE inhibitors: These medications reduce afterload and decrease SVR, improving CO.
   • Beta-blockers: These medications reduce heart rate and contractility, reducing the workload on the heart.
   • Diuretics: These medications reduce fluid overload and decrease SVR, improving CO.
   • ARBs: These medications reduce afterload and decrease SVR, improving CO.

• **Clinical Trade-offs:** The management of CHF involves several clinical trade-offs, including the balance between reducing symptoms and improving quality of life versus reducing morbidity and mortality. The clinician must carefully weigh the benefits and risks of each treatment option and tailor the management plan to the individual patient's needs.
